posts.meta_desc: Practical guide to a stock market internship for beginners in India: screening NSE and BSE stocks, reading annual reports and writing research reports.
posts.summary: What beginners should look for in an online stock market training internship in India: learning how exchanges work, screening NSE and BSE universes on delayed data, reading annual reports, and writing a structured company study.
sections: Why most beginners start in the wrong place

When college students search for a stock market internship for beginners in India, they often encounter two unhelpful extremes. On one side are informal groups that equate market learning with watching intraday price ticks, indicator crossovers, or unverified social-media commentary. On the other side are purely theoretical university syllabi that define capital market terms from outdated textbooks without ever opening a real company filing on the National Stock Exchange (NSE) or BSE.

Professional analytical work in capital markets looks very different from both of those extremes. At institutional research desks, mutual funds, credit rating agencies, and corporate finance teams, analysts spend the majority of their time reading primary corporate disclosures, spreading five to ten years of audited financial statements, comparing operating ratios across industry peers, and documenting their reasoning in structured written reports.

A credible beginner training program should teach you that process from day one. Rather than asking you to predict tomorrow's index movement, it should train you to answer concrete, verifiable questions about a listed business: How does the company generate revenue? What are its major operating cost drivers? How much working capital does it require to grow? And how does its balance-sheet leverage compare with competitors in the same sector?
Training program vs. employment internship: understanding the distinction

Before enrolling in any online program, beginners should understand the difference between an employment role at a regulated brokerage or asset manager and a structured educational training internship. In India, many students in their second or third year of B.Com, BBA, BA Economics, or first year of MBA do not yet have a portfolio of analytical work to show an employer. Because research desks evaluate candidates based on actual writing and spreadsheet samples, students need a structured environment to build their first complete company model and equity research report.

The Harion Equity Research Internship Program is designed explicitly as an online educational training program. Participants have free self-paced access to 40 structured classroom lessons and use our public Market Analysis Learning Lab (Research Scanner) to study NSE and BSE universes, with an optional ₹500 certificate fee upon mentor review of the completed research report. Keeping this distinction transparent helps students evaluate programs honestly: your goal in a beginner training program is to acquire verifiable analytical skills and produce a concrete portfolio artifact.
Step 1: Learning how Indian equity universes are organized

A beginner's first week in market research should focus on market structure and universe segmentation. Thousands of companies are listed across NSE and BSE, ranging from multi-trillion-rupee benchmark constituents to small niche manufacturers. Trying to study individual companies at random leads to confusion because accounting norms, liquidity profiles, and business cycles vary widely across market capitalizations.

Inside the Harion Research Scanner, beginners start by observing eight structured universes on delayed End-of-Day (EOD) data: NIFTY 50, NIFTY 200, NIFTY 500, All NSE Stocks, BSE Large Cap, BSE Mid Cap, BSE Small Cap, and All BSE Stocks. Studying a universe systematically teaches you how index constituents are grouped, why liquidity and delivery volume matter when observing historical price action, and how sector weights differ between large-cap benchmarks and broader mid-cap or small-cap segments.
Step 2: Moving from market screening to financial statements

Once you understand how a stock universe is organized, the next skill is using rule-based screening filters to shortlist companies for deeper reading. A stock scanner is not a vending machine for stock ideas; it is an organizational lens that helps an analyst narrow 500 companies down to 10 or 15 peers that share specific financial or structural characteristics.

For example, a beginner studying the Indian consumer durables or industrial manufacturing sector might use the Research Scanner's Financial Ratio Study module to observe how Return on Capital Employed (ROCE), Operating Profit Margin (OPM %), and Debt-to-Equity ratios vary across companies in the NIFTY 500 universe. When you see that one company maintains a 22% ROCE with minimal debt while a direct competitor earns 11% ROCE with higher borrowings, you have found an analytical question worth investigating in the annual reports.

This transition—from a quantitative screen to reading primary filings—is the core habit that separates disciplined analysts from casual observers. You never stop at the ratio shown on a screen; you open the company's audited annual report to verify how that ratio was produced.
Step 3: Reading the three financial statements together

Beginners often learn the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement as three separate chapters in an accounting class. In real equity research, the three statements form a single interlocking system. Revenue recognized on the income statement either arrives as cash in the bank or sits on the balance sheet as trade receivables. Inventory purchased for production either flows through cost of goods sold or remains tied up on the balance sheet, absorbing working capital.

During a 60-day structured research project, beginners learn to spread at least five years of historical numbers across all three statements simultaneously. You calculate receivable days, inventory days, and payable days to see whether reported net income is supported by Cash Flow from Operations (CFO). You also read the Notes to Accounts to check depreciation policies, related-party transactions, and contingent liabilities such as pending tax or legal disputes.
Step 4: Writing an educational equity research report

The culmination of a beginner stock market training program should always be a written document. Writing forces precision: vague impressions about a 'good company' or a 'growing sector' quickly fall apart when you have to support every paragraph with data from annual reports, industry trade bodies, or exchange filings.

In our program workflow—Screen, Model, Write, Review, Publish—every participant writes a complete educational case study covering five standard sections: Business Overview, Industry and Competitive Structure, Financial Statement Analysis, Valuation Context, and Key Risks. Mentors review drafts during weekly sessions to check whether assumptions are stated clearly and whether risks are treated with the same rigor as growth drivers. By the end of the 60 days, you leave not with vague familiarity, but with a finished spreadsheet model and a written report you can discuss line by line in any academic or analyst interview.

sections: Why finance recruiters look past generic certificates

Every semester, thousands of B.Com, BBA, BMS, BA Economics, and MBA students in India search for a finance internship with certificate for students to fulfill college credit requirements or strengthen their resumes. Yet anyone who has sat on a finance interview panel knows a simple truth: a PDF certificate by itself tells an interviewer almost nothing about what you can actually do.

When a hiring manager or faculty evaluator sees a line on your CV stating that you completed a finance training program, their very first question is practical: 'Walk me through the company you analysed, show me the spreadsheet model you built, and explain the key risks you identified in its balance sheet.' If the program consisted only of watching passive videos and clicking through a multiple-choice quiz, the conversation ends there.
A certificate has value only when it represents a verified deliverable—a tangible piece of analytical work that you researched, calculated, wrote, and revised under review.
What makes a finance training program credible

When evaluating an online finance training internship in India, students should examine four specific criteria before enrolling: transparency of structure and fees, access to real analytical tools, depth of primary-source work, and mentor review standards.

First, look for complete clarity on what the program is. At Harion Research, our Equity Research Internship Program is a 60-day online training program where all 40 self-paced classroom lessons are free to study, weekly live mentor review sessions guide your progress, and the optional verified completion certificate carries a transparent ₹500 fee upon submission and review of your final report. There are no hidden tiers or vague promises.

Second, check whether you work with real datasets. Rather than studying hypothetical 'Company X' textbook examples, participants use the Harion Market Analysis Learning Lab (Research Scanner) to screen listed NSE and BSE companies using delayed End-of-Day market data and reported financial ratios, and then download real audited annual reports for their chosen company.
The four artifacts every finance student should build before graduating

Whether you plan to apply for equity research roles, credit analysis, corporate finance, wealth management, or higher studies such as CFA or MBA Finance, completing a structured 60-day training project should leave you with four specific artifacts alongside your certificate:

1. A multi-year historical financial model: A clean workbook containing five years of income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement data extracted directly from a listed company's annual reports, complete with common-size percentages, working-capital days, and DuPont ROE/ROCE decomposition.

2. A peer-group comparison table: A structured benchmark comparing your chosen company against three to five listed industry competitors across operating margins, asset turnover, leverage (Debt-to-Equity and Interest Coverage), and historical valuation multiples (P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA).

3. A sector and business model note: A concise written explanation of how the industry operates—what drives demand, what raw materials or employee costs determine margins, and how regulation affects competition.

4. A complete educational equity research report: A 10-to-15-page report assembling your business, sector, financial, valuation, and risk analysis into a single cohesive document reviewed by a mentor.
How to fit a 60-day training internship around university exams

One of the most common concerns for undergraduate and postgraduate students is balancing an intensive analytical project with college lectures, internal assessments, and semester exams. A well-structured online training program solves this by separating conceptual learning from project execution.

In the Harion Classroom, the 40 lessons are broken into focused, self-paced modules covering research methodology, financial statement analysis, sector mapping, valuation logic, and report documentation. Students typically dedicate four to six hours per week: studying two to three classroom modules on weekdays, applying those concepts to their chosen listed company's annual report over the weekend, and attending the weekly live mentor session to get feedback on their spreadsheet and draft sections.
How to present your research project and certificate on your CV

Once you finish your report and receive your verified certificate, how you describe the work on your resume matters. Avoid generic phrases. Instead, state the exact analytical tasks you executed. For example: 'Completed the 60-day Equity Research Internship Program (online training) at Harion Research; screened NSE/BSE sector peers in the Research Scanner, built a 5-year historical financial statement and ratio model on [Listed Company Name], and authored a mentor-reviewed educational equity research report analyzing working-capital cycles, ROCE drivers, and balance-sheet risks.'

Attach a link to your published portfolio report right next to your certificate. When an interviewer can click a link and read your 12-page analysis of an Indian listed business, your certificate becomes backed by undeniable evidence of skill.

posts.h1: Finance Internship Project Ideas: 7 Practical Equity & Financial Analysis Topics
posts.meta_desc: Seven practical finance internship project ideas for B.Com, BBA and MBA students in India using NSE/BSE filings and the Harion Research Scanner.
posts.summary: Struggling to choose a topic for your college finance project or equity research training report? Here are seven structured, data-driven project frameworks using real Indian company filings.
sections: What separates a strong finance project from a weak one

Every year, thousands of B.Com, BBA, BMS, and MBA Finance students in India must submit a summer internship report or capstone finance project. Too often, students pick overly broad topics like 'A Study on Mutual Funds in India' or 'Overview of the Indian Banking Sector' and fill 50 pages with copied definitions and pie charts from secondary websites.

Faculty examiners and industry interviewers immediately recognize when a project lacks original analytical work. A strong finance internship project is narrow, specific, and grounded in primary financial data. Instead of writing about an entire economy in generalities, you select a specific listed company or a tight cohort of three to five peer companies on the NSE or BSE, extract five years of audited financial statements, and test a clear analytical question.
Below are seven concrete finance internship project ideas that you can execute using public annual reports and the Harion Market Analysis Learning Lab (Research Scanner).
Project Idea 1: DuPont ROE & ROCE Decomposition Across Sector Peers

Pick three to four listed companies within a single Indian industry—for example, specialty chemicals, auto ancillaries, or fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG). Extract five years of income statements and balance sheets for each company.

Break down Return on Equity (ROE) into its three DuPont components: Net Profit Margin (operating efficiency), Asset Turnover (capital utilization speed), and Financial Leverage (total assets divided by shareholders' equity). Perform a parallel decomposition on Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) using EBIT margin and capital-employed turnover.

Your project report should explain why two companies in the same industry achieve similar headline ROE through completely different paths—for instance, why Company A relies on high brand margins and zero debt while Company B relies on thin margins, rapid inventory turnover, and higher borrowings.
Project Idea 2: Working Capital Cycle & Cash Conversion Study

In capital-intensive sectors such as industrial engineering, building materials, cables and wires, or pharmaceuticals, revenue growth on the income statement does not always translate into cash in the bank. For this project, select a mid-cap or large-cap manufacturing company from the NIFTY 500 universe in the Harion Research Scanner.

Calculate Inventory Days, Trade Receivable Days, and Trade Payable Days across a 5-to-7-year period. Compare the resulting Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) against the ratio of Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) to EBITDA. Investigate the Notes to Accounts to see how raw-material price swings, dealer credit terms, or capacity expansions affected free cash flow generation over the cycle.
Project Idea 3: Capital Allocation & Capex Effectiveness Analysis

When a profitable business generates operating cash flow, management has five choices for deploying that capital: reinvesting in organic capital expenditure (capex), funding working capital, paying down debt, acquiring other businesses, or distributing cash to shareholders via dividends and buybacks.

Track 10 years of Cash Flow Statements for a listed Indian company. Sum total cumulative CFO over the decade and map exactly what percentage went to capex, acquisitions, debt service, and dividends. Then calculate Incremental Return on Capital Employed (the change in EBIT divided by the change in capital employed over multi-year blocks) to evaluate whether management's capital expenditure projects created or diluted economic value.
Project Idea 4: Balance-Sheet Leverage & Interest Coverage Stress Test

Select a cyclical sector such as metals, cement, hospitality, or commercial vehicles. Using the Financial Ratio Study module in the Research Scanner, compare Debt-to-Equity and Interest Coverage ratios across five listed peers.

Go beyond single-year ratios by reading the debt-maturity schedule and borrowing footnotes in each company's annual report. Build a simple sensitivity table in your spreadsheet showing what happens to each company's Interest Coverage Ratio (EBIT divided by Finance Costs) if sector revenue drops by 15% and operating margins compress by 300 basis points—demonstrating risk-first thinking in practice.
Project Idea 5: Revenue Mix & Unit Economics in Indian IT or Healthcare

Service-oriented sectors such as IT services, diagnostic chains, and hospital networks disclose rich operational metrics in their investor presentations and annual reports. For a diagnostic chain or hospital group, track Average Revenue Per Occupied Bed (ARPOB), occupancy rates, average length of stay (ALOS), and brownfield vs. greenfield bed additions. For an IT services company, track client bucket progression, attrition, utilization, and offshore revenue mix. Connect these non-GAAP operating metrics directly to reported operating margins and ROCE.
Project Idea 6: Multi-Factor Price, Volume & Fundamental Regime Study

Using the Market Analysis Learning Lab's historical observation frameworks, study how a cohort of NIFTY 200 companies behaved across distinct market phases (trending, consolidation, and high-volatility phases) on delayed End-of-Day data. Pair these historical price-structure and relative-volume observations with underlying quarterly earnings and margin trends from company filings to document how fundamental operating changes and market structure interact over multi-quarter windows.
Project Idea 7: A Complete Single-Company Equity Research Case Study

The most comprehensive project—and the exact deliverable of the 60-day Harion Equity Research Internship Program—is a full-length educational equity research report on a single listed company. Combining all of the modules above, you screen the universe to select your company, spread five years of financial statements, analyze industry competitiveness, build explicit valuation sensitivity tables, and document key risks under weekly mentor review.

posts.title_tag: Equity Research Analyst Skills & Tools | Harion Research
posts.h1: Equity Research Analyst Skills and Tools: What You Need to Master
posts.meta_desc: Essential skills and tools used by equity research analysts in India: financial statement analysis, stock screening, modelling and report writing.
posts.summary: A practical breakdown of the core skills and software tools every aspiring equity research analyst in India needs—from screening NSE/BSE universes to building clean spreadsheet models and writing clear reports.
sections: The modern equity research stack

Aspiring analysts often wonder whether they need expensive institutional terminals or advanced programming degrees before they can begin studying equity research. While institutional desks use specialized data feeds, the core analytical stack of an equity research analyst rests on four accessible pillars: a structured market and ratio scanner, primary corporate filings from exchanges, disciplined spreadsheet modelling, and clear analytical writing.
Understanding how these tools fit together—and developing the habits to use them without cognitive bias—is far more important than memorizing textbook formulas.
Skill 1: Accounting literacy and forensic reading of filings

Accounting is the language of equity research. An analyst does not need to be a statutory auditor, but you must be able to read an Indian company's consolidated and standalone financial statements under Ind AS (Indian Accounting Standards) with confidence.

Specifically, you need to understand how revenue recognition policies work across sectors, how capitalization of expenses (such as moving operating costs into intangible assets or capital work-in-progress) affects reported EBITDA, how working-capital changes drive divergence between net profit and operating cash flow, and where to locate off-balance-sheet commitments, related-party transactions, and auditor qualifications in the Notes to Accounts.
Skill 2: Systematic universe screening
With over 4,000 companies listed across BSE and NSE, an analyst cannot read annual reports at random. You need a systematic screening tool to filter universes by objective criteria.

In the Harion Market Analysis Learning Lab (Research Scanner), analysts practice multi-factor observation across eight NSE and BSE universes (including NIFTY 50, NIFTY 200, NIFTY 500, and BSE Large, Mid, and Small Cap segments). You learn to combine fundamental filters—such as Return on Capital Employed (ROCE), Return on Equity (ROE), Operating Profit Margin (OPM %), Debt-to-Equity, and trailing P/E or EV/EBITDA—with historical End-of-Day price and volume behaviour.

Crucially, a skilled analyst treats scanner output as a set of questions, not answers. Seeing that a company has a low P/E ratio or high historical revenue growth in a dataset is simply the prompt to open its filings and investigate why.
Skill 3: Clean, auditable financial modelling

A financial model is not judged by how many tabs or complex macros it contains; it is judged by whether another analyst can audit its logic in ten minutes. In our training program, interns learn to build clean, modular spreadsheets that separate raw historical inputs (sourced directly from annual reports), calculated ratios and common-size tables, explicit operating drivers (volume, realization, capacity utilization, margin assumptions), and valuation sensitivity tables.

Every formula should be transparent, hard-coded numbers should never be mixed inside calculation cells, and every historical figure should trace back to a specific page number in the company's annual report.
Skill 4: Industry and competitive mapping

No company operates in a vacuum. A chemical manufacturer's margins depend on crude-linked feedstock prices and global capacity additions; a hospital chain's ROCE depends on bed maturity and payer mix; an auto component maker's revenue depends on original equipment manufacturer (OEM) production schedules and export regulations.

Analysts develop the habit of reading DRHPs (Draft Red Herring Prospectuses of recently listed sector peers, which contain detailed industry chapters), credit rating rationales from agencies like CRISIL, ICRA, and CARE, and quarterly investor transcripts to map the competitive landscape.
Skill 5: Evidence-based writing and risk analysis

The final product of equity research is written prose. Whether you are writing a two-page quarterly update or a fifteen-page initiation case study, your writing must be calm, precise, and structured. Avoid promotional adjectives and market jargon. State the evidence, show the historical numbers, explain the assumptions behind your valuation range, and dedicate an entire section to the specific operational, financial, and regulatory risks that could invalidate your analysis.

posts.title_tag: How to Read an Annual Report in India | Harion Research
posts.h1: How to Read an Indian Company Annual Report for Equity Research
posts.meta_desc: Step-by-step guide to reading an Indian corporate annual report: MD&A, Auditor's Report, CARO, financial statements and Notes to Accounts.
posts.summary: A 300-page annual report can feel overwhelming to a student. Here is the exact sequence analysts use to read Indian annual reports efficiently and extract what matters.
sections: Why you should not read a 300-page annual report from page 1 to 300

Modern annual reports of listed Indian companies frequently run between 250 and 450 pages. The first 30 pages are typically filled with glossy photographs, marketing slogans, and award summaries. If a student tries to read the PDF linearly from cover to cover, fatigue sets in long before reaching the audited financial statements and footnotes where the essential facts live.

Experienced equity research analysts read an annual report in a deliberate, non-linear sequence designed to understand the business model first, check governance and audit quality second, and dissect the financial numbers and footnotes third.
Stage 1: Management Discussion & Analysis (MD&A) and Business Overview

Start by locating the Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) section and the corporate overview tables. Read three years of MD&A sections side by side (for example, FY24, FY25, and FY26). Reading multiple years sequentially reveals whether management's stated operational plans actually materialized in subsequent years or whether challenges were repeatedly blamed on external factors.

Extract the concrete operational facts: What are the distinct business segments? What share of revenue comes from domestic sales versus exports? What is the installed manufacturing capacity and capacity utilization percentage? What are the primary raw materials or cost components?
Stage 2: Independent Auditor's Report and CARO Disclosures

Before trusting a single number on the income statement, turn directly to the Independent Auditor's Report (specifically for the Consolidated Financial Statements, and also check Standalone). Look for whether the audit opinion is unmodified (clean) or qualified, and read the 'Key Audit Matters' (KAM) and 'Emphasis of Matter' paragraphs.

In India, the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order (CARO) annexure is a goldmine for analysts. It explicitly reports whether physical inventory verification revealed discrepancies, whether undisputed statutory dues (GST, provident fund, income tax) are in arrears, whether the company has defaulted on loan repayments, and whether funds raised for short-term purposes were used for long-term investments.
Stage 3: Corporate Governance and Board's Report

In the Board's Report and Corporate Governance section, examine promoter shareholding trends, managerial remuneration relative to net profit, board independence, and related-party disclosures. Check whether key committees (Audit Committee, Nomination and Remuneration Committee) are chaired by independent directors and whether there have been frequent resignations of auditors, chief financial officers, or independent board members.
Stage 4: The Three Primary Financial Statements
Now open the Consolidated Financial Statements (and compare against Standalone to understand what subsidiaries or joint ventures contribute):

1. Balance Sheet: Examine the structure of non-current assets (Property, Plant & Equipment, Capital Work-in-Progress, Goodwill, Intangible Assets), working-capital items (Inventories, Trade Receivables, Cash and Bank Balances vs. Trade Payables), and financing (Equity Share Capital, Other Equity/Reserves, Long-Term and Short-Term Borrowings, Lease Liabilities).

2. Statement of Profit and Loss: Track Revenue from Operations separately from Other Income (such as treasury interest or one-off asset sales). Calculate gross margin (after cost of materials consumed and changes in inventory), employee benefit expenses, other expenses, EBITDA, finance costs, depreciation, and tax rate.

3. Cash Flow Statement: Compare Cash Flow from Operating Activities (after working-capital adjustments and taxes paid) with reported EBITDA and Net Profit. Examine Cash Flow from Investing Activities (capex, inter-corporate deposits, acquisitions) and Financing Activities (debt raised/repaid, interest paid, dividends).
Stage 5: The Notes to Accounts (where the real details live)
Every line on the balance sheet and income statement references a Note number. Analysts spend more time in the Notes to Accounts than on the summary statements. Pay close attention to:
- Accounting Policies (Note 1/2): Revenue recognition timing, inventory valuation method, and useful life assumptions for depreciation.
- Trade Receivables Ageing Schedule: Shows what portion of receivables is overdue by more than 6 months, 1 year, or 2 years, and how much credit-loss provision has been made.
- Borrowings Footnote: Lists interest rates, repayment schedules, security pledged, and any covenant terms.

- Contingent Liabilities & Commitments: Details pending tax demands, bank guarantees, and letter-of-credit exposures that do not sit on the balance sheet today but could become cash outflows tomorrow.
- Related-Party Transactions (RPT): Lists sales, purchases, rent, loans, or guarantees between the listed company and promoter-owned entities.

posts.title_tag: Financial Modelling Basics for Interns | Harion Research
posts.h1: Financial Modelling Basics for Interns: Spreading Statements, Ratios and Cash Flows
posts.meta_desc: Learn financial modelling basics for equity research internships in India: historical spreads, working-capital schedules, ROCE/ROE and valuation.
posts.summary: How to build a clean, auditable three-statement financial analysis workbook from scratch using reported Indian corporate filings.
sections: What a financial model actually is in equity research

Many students think financial modelling means memorizing keyboard shortcuts or building complicated thirty-tab workbooks full of circular references. In practical equity research, a financial model is simply a structured numerical representation of how a business operates—built so that an analyst can test how changes in volume, pricing, costs, and working capital affect earnings, cash flows, and balance-sheet health.
A concise, well-organized five-tab workbook that accurately reflects a company's unit economics is far more useful than a sprawling template you do not fully understand.
Step 1: Setting up the historical three-statement spread

Every reliable model starts with at least five years of audited historical data entered directly from the company's annual reports (typically in ₹ Crore or ₹ Million, kept consistent throughout the workbook). Never rely solely on automated exports without checking them against the actual PDF filing, because automated databases frequently lump operating expenses together or misclassify one-time items.

Keep your layout clean: place historical fiscal years (e.g., FY22 through FY26) in consecutive columns from left to right. Separate the Income Statement, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow Statement clearly, and include an explicit balance-sheet check row (Total Assets minus Total Equity and Liabilities = 0) so any data-entry error is caught immediately.
Step 2: Building common-size and ratio schedules

Directly below or alongside your historical statements, build a common-size schedule expressing every income statement line item as a percentage of Revenue from Operations. Seeing raw-material cost move from 54.2% of revenue to 58.7% over three years immediately highlights gross-margin compression that raw rupee numbers can obscure during periods of high top-line growth.
Next, construct your core analytical ratio block across four categories:
1. Profitability & Capital Efficiency: Gross Margin %, EBITDA Margin %, EBIT Margin %, Net Profit Margin %, Return on Equity (ROE), and Return on Capital Employed (ROCE).
2. Working Capital & Activity: Inventory Days, Receivable Days, Payable Days, Net Cash Conversion Cycle, and Fixed Asset Turnover.
3. Solvency & Liquidity: Total Debt-to-Equity, Net Debt-to-EBITDA, Current Ratio, and Interest Coverage Ratio (EBIT / Finance Costs).
4. Cash Conversion Quality: Operating Cash Flow (CFO) divided by EBITDA, and Free Cash Flow (CFO minus Capital Expenditure).
Step 3: Revenue and cost driver decomposition

Rather than projecting revenue as a flat percentage growth number, break revenue down into its underlying physical or operational drivers whenever disclosures permit. For a cement or steel manufacturer, model installed capacity (in million tonnes), capacity utilization %, sales volume, and average realization per tonne. For a retail or restaurant chain, model store count, new store additions, and same-store sales growth (SSSG).

Do the same on the cost side by separating variable costs (raw materials, freight, power and fuel linked to production volume) from semi-fixed costs (employee salaries, administrative overhead, lease rentals).
Step 4: Working capital, capex and depreciation schedules

To connect projections across the three statements, build supporting schedules for working capital and fixed assets. Use historical Receivable Days, Inventory Days, and Payable Days to estimate how much incremental working capital will be absorbed as revenue changes. In the fixed-asset schedule, link opening Gross Block, annual capital expenditure additions, and depreciation rates to compute closing Net Block and annual depreciation expense.
Step 5: Valuation sensitivity tables (process over point targets)

In the final tab of your workbook, summarize peer valuation multiples (P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA) and discounted cash flow (DCF) sensitivity tables. Instead of presenting a single point estimate as a 'true value', build a two-way sensitivity matrix showing how implied enterprise value varies across different discount rates (WACC) and terminal growth or operating margin assumptions. This keeps uncertainty visible and grounds your written research report in transparent math.

posts.title_tag: What Goes Into an Equity Research Report | Harion Research
posts.h1: What Goes Into an Equity Research Report: Structure, Evidence and Valuation
posts.meta_desc: The structure of an equity research report: business overview, industry analysis, financial statement analysis, valuation sensitivity and risks.
posts.summary: A comprehensive guide to the sections of an institutional-style educational equity research report—and how students can write one that demonstrates real analytical depth.
sections: Why structure matters in equity research

A well-written equity research report lets a reader verify your reasoning at every step. Whether the reader is a portfolio manager, a university professor, or an interview panelist, they should never have to guess where a number came from or why you reached a particular analytical conclusion.

Professional reports follow a disciplined, familiar architecture so readers can inspect the business model, sector context, financial history, valuation assumptions, and downside risks systematically. In the Harion Equity Research Internship Program, every participant authors a complete educational case study following this exact structure—without speculative price targets or buy/sell ratings.
Section 1: Executive Summary & Company Snapshot

The opening page of your report sets the factual context. It includes the company's NSE/BSE ticker, sector classification, market capitalization segment, and a concise summary table of key historical metrics (5-year revenue and profit CAGR, latest ROE, ROCE, Operating Margin, and Debt-to-Equity ratio sourced from reported filings).

The executive summary states the central analytical questions of the report in three to four crisp paragraphs: What does the business do, what structural drivers or headwinds shape its economics, and what are the primary financial observations from its multi-year statements?
Section 2: Business Overview & Unit Economics

Before discussing stock multiples or charts, explain how the business actually works on the ground. Break down revenue by product line, service vertical, and geography (domestic vs. export). Explain who the customers are (B2B industrial buyers, government tenders, or retail consumers), how products are distributed, and what inputs (raw materials, power, skilled labor) drive the cost structure.
Include a summary of capacity, plant locations, and management background based on the company's Annual Report and corporate disclosures.
Section 3: Industry Structure & Competitive Positioning

Next, place the company inside its industry context. How fragmented or consolidated is the sector? Is demand cyclical (tied to interest rates, monsoons, or capex cycles) or non-cyclical? What regulatory frameworks, import duties, or environmental norms govern the industry?

Include a structured peer-comparison table benchmarking your subject company against three to five listed competitors on NSE/BSE using data from the Harion Research Scanner and primary filings. Compare scale, operating margins, asset turnover, working-capital days, and ROCE to show where the company holds operational strengths or weaknesses relative to peers.
Section 4: Financial Statement & Cash Flow Analysis
This is the analytical core of the report. Rather than merely listing ratios in a table without commentary, explain what changed over the last five years and why:
- Income Statement Trends: Discuss revenue growth drivers (volume vs. price realization) and gross/operating margin movements.
- Balance Sheet & Working Capital: Analyze Debt-to-Equity, Interest Coverage, Inventory Days, and Receivable Days. Highlight any buildup in capital work-in-progress or intangible assets.
- Cash Flow Conversion: Compare cumulative EBITDA and Net Profit against cumulative Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) and Free Cash Flow (FCF). Explain how capital expenditure was funded.
Section 5: Valuation Context & Sensitivity Analysis

In an educational research report, valuation is presented as a study of expectations and sensitivities, never as investment advice. Compare the company's current P/E, P/B, and EV/EBITDA multiples against its own 5-year historical range and against the peer-group median. If you include a discounted cash flow (DCF) framework, state every assumption explicitly—revenue growth, terminal margin, capex intensity, and discount rate—and show a sensitivity table illustrating how the output shifts when those assumptions change.
Section 6: Key Risks, Governance & Limitations

Every rigorous report finishes with an honest examination of what could go wrong. Document specific operational risks (raw-material volatility, customer concentration, project execution delays), financial risks (refinancing, foreign-exchange exposure, contingent liabilities), and governance considerations (related-party transactions, promoter pledges, or audit remarks). Presenting conclusions strictly as educational analysis—backed by citations to primary filings—demonstrates mature, risk-first thinking.

sections: What an equity research analyst actually does day to day

Equity research analysts study listed companies and industries, build financial statement models, evaluate business risks, and write detailed research reports for institutional investors, buy-side funds, family offices, or research desks. Contrary to popular media depictions, the role is not about fast-paced screen trading; it is a quiet, reading-and-writing-intensive profession that rewards curiosity, accounting rigor, and clear reasoning.

In India, equity research roles exist across sell-side institutional brokerages, buy-side asset management companies (mutual funds, PMS, AIFs), independent research platforms, credit rating agencies, and global capability centres (GCCs) supporting international financial institutions.
Step 1: Build a rock-solid foundation in accounting and corporate finance

A degree in commerce (B.Com), management (BBA/MBA), economics, engineering, or chartered accountancy provides a helpful starting point, though no single undergraduate degree is mandatory if you can demonstrate analytical competence. Your first priority must be mastering financial accounting.

Learn how an Indian company's balance sheet, statement of profit and loss, and cash flow statement connect under Ind AS. Practice calculating and interpreting Return on Capital Employed (ROCE), Return on Equity (ROE), working-capital days, free cash flow, and solvency ratios from real annual reports rather than textbook summaries.
Step 2: Practice systematic screening across NSE and BSE universes

To develop sector awareness, start studying how metrics vary across Indian industries. Use a public educational tool like the Harion Market Analysis Learning Lab (Research Scanner) to observe NIFTY 50, NIFTY 200, NIFTY 500, and BSE Large, Mid, and Small Cap universes on delayed End-of-Day data.

Compare capital-light sectors (such as IT services or FMCG) against capital-intensive sectors (such as cement, metals, power, or specialty chemicals). Observing how margins, asset turnover, and leverage behave across different industries builds the mental benchmarks every analyst needs.
Step 3: Understand relevant certifications (NISM Series XV, NISM VIII, CFA)
In India, regulatory and professional certifications signal commitment and domain knowledge:

- NISM-Series-XV (Research Analyst Certification Examination): Conducted by the National Institute of Securities Markets (a SEBI institute), this is the mandatory certification required for individuals employed as registered research analysts in India. Its syllabus covers fundamentals of research, economic and industry analysis, corporate actions, valuation principles, and SEBI (Research Analysts) Regulations.

- NISM-Series-VIII (Equity Derivatives Certification Examination): Widely required across broking, dealing, risk management, and capital market operations roles to demonstrate understanding of futures, options, clearing, settlement, and derivatives regulation.
- CFA (Chartered Financial Analyst) or CA: Valuable long-term credentials for deep financial statement analysis, portfolio management, and global valuation standards.
Step 4: Complete a structured training internship and build a report portfolio

Certifications prove you passed an exam; a research portfolio proves you can do the job. Before applying to analyst openings, write at least two to three complete, 10-to-15-page company research reports accompanied by your own three-statement spreadsheet models.

If you want structured guidance and feedback while building your first report, the Harion Equity Research Internship Program (a 60-day online training program with 40 free self-paced classroom lessons, weekly live mentor sessions, and an optional ₹500 certificate fee upon report review) walks you through the entire workflow: screening a company in the Research Scanner, spreading five years of filings, analyzing the sector, and writing a mentor-reviewed educational research report.
Step 5: How to approach equity research interviews

When you apply for research internships or junior analyst roles, attach your completed research report and financial model directly to your application email. During interviews, be prepared to defend every assumption in your model, explain the unit economics of the industry you studied, and discuss the top three risks that could hurt the company's cash flows. Demonstrating disciplined process over prediction is the clearest way to stand out.

sections: What is the NISM Series VIII Equity Derivatives Certification?

The NISM-Series-VIII: Equity Derivatives Certification Examination is an official certification administered by the National Institute of Securities Markets (NISM) under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) certification regulations. It is designed to establish a common minimum knowledge benchmark for associated persons functioning as approved users and sales personnel of trading members of an equity derivatives exchange.

For commerce, finance, and MBA students in India, passing NISM Series VIII is a widely recognized credential when applying for roles in capital markets operations, institutional and retail broking desks, wealth management, risk management, and derivatives dealing.
Exam pattern, duration, passing marks and negative marking
Understanding the exact test mechanics is critical before you begin studying, especially because of the negative marking rule:
- Total Questions: 100 multiple-choice questions.
- Maximum Marks: 100 marks (1 mark per question).
- Exam Duration: 120 minutes (2 hours).
- Passing Score: 60% (60 marks out of 100).
- Negative Marking: Yes—25% of the marks assigned to a question (0.25 marks deducted for every wrong answer).
- Certificate Validity: 3 years from the date of passing.

- Exam Fee: NISM typically lists the test fee at ₹1,500 plus applicable taxes/charges; candidates should always verify the latest fee and slot availability directly on the official NISM portal (nism.ac.in) before registering.
Complete NISM Series VIII syllabus breakdown
Questions on the exam are drawn directly from the official NISM Equity Derivatives workbook across ten core subject areas:

1. Basics of Derivatives: Definition of derivatives, history of derivatives markets, Indian derivatives market structure, market participants (hedgers, speculators, arbitrageurs), and OTC vs. exchange-traded contracts.
2. Understanding Index: How stock market indices (such as NIFTY 50 and SENSEX) are constructed—free-float market capitalization weighting, price weighting, impact cost, and index management.
3. Introduction to Forwards and Futures: Forward vs. futures contracts, contract specifications (lot size, tick size, expiry cycle, open interest, volume), payoff charts for long and short futures.

4. Pricing of Futures & Hedging: The cost-of-carry model, concept of basis, contango and backwardation, cash-and-carry arbitrage, and using index/stock futures to hedge equity portfolios (including beta adjustment).

5. Introduction to Options & Option Pricing: Call and put options, American vs. European style, moneyness (ITM, ATM, OTM), intrinsic value vs. time value, put-call parity, Determinants of option prices (spot price, strike, volatility, time to expiry, interest rates, dividends), and the Option Greeks (Delta, Gamma, Theta, Vega, Rho).
6. Option Trading Strategies: Payoff profiles, breakeven points, maximum gain and maximum loss calculations for protective puts, covered calls, bull/bear spreads, straddles, and strangles.
7. Trading Mechanism: Order types (market, limit, stop-loss, IOC), corporate action adjustments on lots and strikes.

8. Introduction to Clearing and Settlement System: Role of the Clearing Corporation, clearing members vs. trading members, daily mark-to-market (MTM) settlement, final settlement, physical delivery vs. cash settlement, and risk containment measures (Initial Margin, SPAN Margin, Exposure Margin, VaR, liquid net worth).
9. Legal and Regulatory Environment: Relevant provisions of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act (SCRA), SEBI Act, position limits for clients/trading members/FPIs, and surveillance.

10. Accounting, Taxation & Sales Practices: Basic accounting treatment of futures and options, taxation of derivatives transactions as business income, client onboarding (KYC, Risk Disclosure Document), and investor grievance redressal.
Why candidates fail—and how to handle the 25% negative marking

The most common reason candidates miss the 60% mark by 2 or 3 points is blind guessing. If a candidate knows 56 questions accurately and guesses randomly on the remaining 44 questions, statistical probability yields roughly 11 right answers (+11 marks) and 33 wrong answers (-8.25 marks), leaving them right on the razor's edge—or below 60 if luck runs against them.

Equally important are numerical payoff and margin questions. The exam regularly tests numerical problems on futures hedging using portfolio beta, option spread breakeven points, mark-to-market daily cash flows, and liquid net worth after margin deductions. Practicing these calculations by hand is essential.
A structured 30-day preparation plan

Week 1 (Units 1–4): Read the official NISM workbook chapters on derivatives basics, index construction, impact cost, and futures pricing/hedging. Practice all end-of-chapter numerical problems on cost-of-carry and beta hedging.

Week 2 (Units 5–6): Master options fundamentals, the Greeks, and option strategy payoffs. Draw payoff diagrams and calculate maximum loss/gain and breakeven points for every standard spread without looking at formulas.

Week 3 (Units 7–10): Study trading mechanisms, clearing and settlement (memorize liquid net worth requirements, SPAN + Exposure margin rules, and position limits), regulatory provisions, and investor protection.

Week 4 (Full-length timed mocks & revision): Take at least three 100-question, 120-minute mock exams under strict negative-marking rules. Review every incorrect answer and skip any question on exam day where you cannot eliminate at least two options. If you want structured coaching with twice-weekly live doubt sessions and three scored mocks, see our 30-day NISM Series VIII Preparation program on the Specialized Programs page.
